summary: A snapshot of the state of standardization of Internet protocols as of July 22, 2004. It lists official protocol standards and Best Current Practice RFCs but is not a complete index to the RFC series. It obsoletes RFC 3600. It is historic and has been replaced by RFC 5000.

eli5.summary: This is a report card showing which rules were official as of one particular day in 2004. Rule books change, so it is out of date now. RFC 5000 replaced it.

subtitle: A snapshot of official Internet protocol standards as of July 2004.

tldr.problem: The Internet standards track is constantly evolving, with protocols moving from proposed to draft to full standard, being obsoleted, or being moved to historic status. Engineers need to know which protocols are official standards at any given time.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3700 is STD 1, a published snapshot of the Internet Official Protocol Standards list as of July 22, 2004. It categorizes protocols into Standard Protocols (full standards), Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, and Best Current Practice documents.
tldr.outcome: A point-in-time reference showing which Internet protocols were official at a specific date. This became historic and was replaced by RFC 5000, which provides updated guidance on finding current standards.

today: RFC 3700 is Historic as a snapshot of July 2004 standards. It has been superseded by RFC 5000, which points readers to the continuously updated standards list maintained at the RFC Editor web site. For current information on which protocols are standard, draft standard, or proposed, consult http://www.rfc-editor.org/rfcxx00.html.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3700 documents the state of Internet protocol standardization as determined by the IETF as of July 22, 2004. It is published as STD 1 (Standard Track Document 1) and serves as a catalog of all official protocol standards and Best Current Practice documents.

The RFC lists protocols organized by their standardization level: Standard Protocols that are required or recommended for Internet use; Draft Standard protocols under active consideration; Proposed Standard protocols recently advanced; and Experimental protocols. It also lists Best Current Practice (BCP) documents that provide operational guidance but are not protocols. It explicitly excludes Informational and Historic RFCs.

The memo is updated daily on the RFC Editor web site at http://www.rfc-editor.org/rfcxx00.html. This document is a snapshot, not a complete index to all RFCs.
sections.eli5: This document lists which Internet communication rules were officially blessed as 'standard' on one specific day in 2004. It is organized like a filing system: here are the fully approved rules, here are the ones being tested, here are the recommended practices.

sections.title: Protocol Levels and Organization
sections.content:
The RFC describes protocols in six main categories:

Standard Protocols are required or strongly recommended for use on the Internet. They are ordered both by STD number (which groups related protocols together) and by RFC number. Examples include TCP (RFC 793, STD 7), UDP (RFC 768, STD 6), and IP (RFC 791, STD 5).

Draft Standard Protocols have significant implementation and deployment but have not yet reached full standard status. The RFC 3700 list includes protocols such as HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2616), IPv6 (RFC 2460), and DHCP (RFC 2131).

Proposed Standard Protocols include many protocols under active development and standardization, such as BGP-4, SIP, and various MIB definitions.

Experimental and Best Current Practice protocols complete the catalog, including reliability guidelines and testing frameworks for multicast transport protocols.
sections.eli5: Protocols are sorted into five bins: officially approved, almost approved, being considered, experimental, and best practices. Each category tells you how much the IETF trusts it.

sections.title: Core Internet Standards
sections.content:
The document lists fundamental standards that form the backbone of the Internet: IP and ICMP (RFC 791 and 792, STD 5) provide basic packet routing and error reporting; UDP (RFC 768, STD 6) and TCP (RFC 793, STD 7) provide transport-layer communication (UDP for simple messages, TCP for reliable streams).

Domain name infrastructure is covered by DNS RFCs 1034 and 1035 (STD 13). Mail protocols include SMTP (RFC 821, STD 10), POP3 (RFC 1939, STD 53), and message format (RFC 822, STD 11). Routing protocols include RIP Version 2 (RFC 2453, STD 56) and OSPF (RFC 2328, STD 54). Management protocols include SNMP and its related frameworks.

The list also includes many auxiliary protocols such as FTP, TELNET, NTP, and DHCP, as well as transmission standards for IP over various link technologies (Ethernet, PPP, FDDI, ATM, Frame Relay).
sections.eli5: This section is like the instruction manual's main chapters: how to route packets (IP), how to send messages reliably (TCP), quickly (UDP), how to find addresses (DNS), how to send email, and so on.

sections.title: Draft and Proposed Standards
sections.content:
RFC 3700 lists 50+ Draft Standard protocols that have significant deployment but have not yet been advanced to full standard. These include IPv6 (RFC 2460), ICMPv6 (RFC 2463), HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2616), and various MIME and email extensions.

Proposed Standards (Section 3.4) include newer protocols such as S/MIME (RFC 3851), Mobile IP extensions, voice and video MIME types, new encryption algorithms, and MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) related protocols. This section shows active work on emerging technologies.

The document notes changes from the previous edition with asterisks, so readers can track which protocols have been promoted, moved to historic status, or newly added.
sections.eli5: These are the rules that almost everyone uses but the IETF hasn't officially blessed yet, or the brand-new rules people are testing. It shows the standards pipeline.

sections.title: Access and Resources
sections.content:
The RFC includes contact information for Internet organizations (IAB, IETF, IRTF, IANA) and methods to retrieve current standards information: the RFC Editor web site at http://www.rfc-editor.org, FTP access to in-notes/std/std1.txt and individual RFC files, and email-based RFC lookup via RFC-INFO@RFC-EDITOR.ORG.

The document explains that while RFC 3700 is a snapshot, the live updated list is maintained daily on the RFC Editor site, and anyone seeking the most current standards information should consult that online version rather than relying on this static document.
sections.eli5: This chapter tells you where to find the official rule book. The web site has the up-to-date list, but if you're offline, you can use FTP or email, or you have this paper snapshot.
